source.title: Distinguishable Deletion: Unifying Knowledge Erasure and Refusal for Large Language Model Unlearning
source.authors: Pu-Ning Yang; Jun-Chi Yu; Qi-Zhou Wang; P. Torr; Bo Han; Xiu-Ying Chen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how its proposed EUA method and several unlearning baselines fare under relearning and prompting attacks, and argues that robustness depends on the unlearning approach and attack. Its results refine the broad claim rather than directly reproducing the named original studies.
record.gate_note: Relevant original results are EUA's attack evaluations in Table 8 and the MUSE-Books relearning comparison in Table 9. The authors also report DR-method detection accuracy and refusal-quality results in Table 2, but those measures do not establish recovery of the forgotten knowledge. Claims about other studies in the related-work discussion are cited results, not rows. The paper tests one-epoch relearning of the unlearning data, not unrelated or loosely related examples.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a new method (EUA) and runs relearning, cross-lingual and jailbreak attacks on EUA and on baseline unlearning methods. Its own numbers bear on B (baselines on MUSE-Books relearn much of the knowledge), E (prompt attacks on EUA on TOFU) and F (EUA's claimed robustness). The attack protocols differ from the original sources, so this is T2 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that EUA achieves superior performance and robustness, with minimal degradation under cross-lingual, relearning and jailbreak attacks. They call relearning substantially more aggressive than prompt attacks, and say EUA degrades noticeably less than KD baselines on MUSE-Books. They also argue that DR methods are fragile because the knowledge stays intact.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes EUA, an energy-boundary unlearning and refusal method; its attack evaluations use one-epoch relearning, translated questions, and jailbreak prompts rather than the original-source methods and measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and benchmark matter: the authors describe relearning as more aggressive than prompt-based attacks. The paper also reports cross-lingual and jailbreak conditions, and compares several different unlearning methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-based refusal (DR) methods on TOFU with LLaMA-3.1-8B lose detection accuracy under tailored attack prompts: ICUL 77.0%→32.0%, VP 71.0%→49.0% (Forget-5%). These methods leave weights untouched, so this is guardrail bypass rather than recovery of unlearned knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time refusal guards for unlearning are bypassed by prompt attacks, whereas weight-level unlearning may not be.

record.code_released: The paper says code is available in supplementary material; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The paper tests one-epoch relearning of the unlearning data, not unrelated or loosely related examples. The TOFU attack results are aggregate EQ scores rather than direct recovery accuracy and have no never-trained comparator. The attack evaluation is limited to the stated benchmarks, models, and attack formats.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's DR-method detection-accuracy and refusal-quality results are not direct measurements of recovered knowledge, so they are not rows. The paper reports no activation-ablation or quantization attack results.

untested.parts: Prompt-based attacks on baseline methods' weights; near-chance accuracy on WMDP under any attack; comparison against a never-trained model.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data, or on a small subset of forgotten facts. Only one epoch on the full forget set was tested.
Entirely untested: no activation ablation or probing of blocked versus deleted knowledge.
Rephrasing, in-context provision of information, and languages other than French. No prompt attacks were run on KD baseline weights, and none on MUSE or WMDP.
EUA was not tested against activation ablation, quantization, subset or unrelated relearning, or multi-epoch relearning. It was not tested on WMDP under attack.

missing.what: Sub-metrics under attack: Prob, ROUGE-L, ES and Truth Ratio. For example, Forget-10% relearn gives Prob 0.0029→0.0266 and Truth Ratio 0.1026→0.1573. These show the size of the recovery directly.
Pre-unlearning LLaMA-3.2-3B TOFU values (Prob 0.9934, ROUGE 0.8616, EQ 0.158 on Forget-10%), needed as the recovery ceiling for the TOFU attack rows.
Original ICLM-7B MUSE-Books values (VerbMem 99.56, KnowMem 58.32), needed to scale the relearning recovery; currently only mentioned in row notes.
Energy-separation AUROC stays 1.0000 under cross-lingual, relearning and jailbreak attacks.
Linguistic Quality (refusal quality) under attacks stays about 0.84–0.865.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 8 'Original' row is EUA without attack, not the pre-unlearning model; EQ there is on a 0–1 scale (Table 1 uses ×10). It is unclear whether the TOFU attack EQ includes EUA's inference-time refusal; the probability-based sub-metrics suggest weight-level evaluation. Relearning uses the whole forget set for one epoch, which is stronger than B's small-subset framing. The setup mentions relearning only on TOFU-10% and MUSE-Books, but Table 8 reports Forget-5% relearning too. No variance is reported for the attack results, and the study is the authors' own evaluation of their own method.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports forgetting and retention metrics and attack evaluations, but does not establish near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy together with retained general ability and attack recovery no greater than in a model that never saw the knowledge.
Tests one-epoch relearning on the unlearning data; does not test unrelated or loosely related examples, or relearning only a subset of forgotten facts.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether EUA blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests jailbreak prompts and French-translated evaluation; does not test ordinary prompt rephrasing, in-context knowledge provision, or other languages.
Tests EUA against the paper's cross-lingual, one-epoch relearning, and jailbreak settings, not against activation ablation or quantization.

relation.reason: Reports its own attack results on EUA and on baseline unlearning methods.

tranche.reason: A new method (EUA) is tested against prompt and relearning attacks, and baselines are relearned too, so the study bears on A, B, E and F. The reader's T5 guess is not needed.

source_check.notes: Table 8's 'Original' row is the unattacked EUA model. Pre-unlearning values are in Table 13 (Prob 0.9934/0.9922) and Table 3 (MUSE-Books 99.56/58.32). Table 9 gives means only, and there is no retrain+relearning control. E.5 says relearning was run on TOFU-10% and MUSE-Books, yet Table 8 also reports a Forget-5% relearn row.

statements.correction: Table 9 reports means only, with no spread (E.4: some tables give only means over seeds 1, 42, 145). No retrained or never-trained model is relearned as a control. NPO VerbMem 10.40 -> 68.58 is about 69% of the pre-unlearning 99.56 (Table 3), ICLM-7B, MUSE-Books, one epoch on the unlearning data.
statements.problem: The 'why' credits this study with controls and uncertainty, but the cited relearning result has neither. Next to the explicit 'no Retrain+fine-tuning control' for 2609.34251, that misleads.

statements.correction: Table 9 (ICLM-7B, MUSE-Books, one-epoch relearning): GradDiff VerbMem 0 -> 36.42 (about 37% of 99.56) and KnowMem 0 -> 43.03 (about 74% of 58.32); WGD 0 -> 28.44 (29%) and 0 -> 30.08 (52%). Both metrics rise for every method; KnowMem recovers a larger share.
statements.problem: In this study recovery shows on both MUSE metrics and only its size differs, so it gives no case where the metric decides whether recovery shows (challenges).
